name: Gartner Hype Cycle
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: The Five-Act Play Every Overhyped Technology Performs
lesson.summary: Gartner's Hype Cycle names the five-stage emotional arc that new technologies tend to travel through in public discourse, from an initial breakthrough to inflated hopes, a disillusioned crash, and eventually a modest, durable plateau of real use.
lesson.body:
In 1995, Gartner analyst Jackie Fenn noticed something curious: nearly every new technology she tracked, from artificial intelligence to virtual reality to the internet itself, seemed to move through the same emotional arc in public discourse, regardless of what the technology actually did. She named it the Hype Cycle, and it has since become one of the most recognizable shapes in technology commentary: a line that rockets up, crashes down, and then climbs slowly back to a modest plateau.

The model names five stages. An Innovation Trigger, usually a research breakthrough or product launch, generates initial media coverage. That coverage snowballs into the Peak of Inflated Expectations, where success stories multiply, often based on a handful of best case pilots rather than typical results. Then reality intrudes: implementations fail to deliver, companies that overpromised go quiet or go under, and press coverage turns skeptical. This is the Trough of Disillusionment. Survivors iterate quietly, producers who understand the real constraints ship better second and third generation products, and adoption climbs the Slope of Enlightenment toward a durable, boring Plateau of Productivity.

The mechanism is not mysterious once you separate two things that get bundled together: expectations and reality. Expectations move fast, driven by press releases, demo videos, and venture funding rounds, because attention is cheap and confirmation feels good. Reality, meaning actual working deployments at scale, moves slowly, gated by engineering, cost curves, and organizational change. The hype cycle is essentially a chart of the widening and then narrowing gap between those two lines.

This is where Technology Adoption Curves become useful. Everett Rogers' diffusion research describes the population of adopters over time: innovators, early adopters, an early majority, a late majority, and laggards, forming a bell curve of cumulative uptake. The Gartner Hype Cycle tracks a different variable, public expectation, but the two curves are related: the Peak of Inflated Expectations typically arrives while real adoption is still confined to innovators and early adopters, well before the technology has proven itself to the more cautious early majority. The gap between those groups is sometimes called the chasm, and a lot of technologies die trying to cross it even while hype is still near its peak.

It is worth being honest about the model's limits. Gartner has never published a rigorous statistical validation showing that most technologies actually trace this exact curve, and critics point out that the categorization is applied after the fact, is not falsifiable in any strict sense, and lumps together technologies with wildly different timelines and risk profiles. Some technologies stall in the trough for decades. Others skip stages entirely. Treat the hype cycle as a vocabulary for organizing skepticism, not a physics equation.

Quantum computing is one of the technologies Gartner tracks explicitly in its own published hype cycle reports, and in recent editions it has generally been placed past its peak and moving toward the trough, with genuinely useful, fault tolerant quantum computers forecast roughly a decade or more away in many editions. Treat that as illustrative of the general shape of these forecasts, not a precise figure, since exact positioning shifts year to year and differs by sub technology. The discipline the model teaches matters more than the exact placement: separate what people say about a technology from what it can currently do.
